definitions.meaning: The first record of information about a cognizable offence, registered by the police under Section 173 of the BNSS. Registering an FIR sets the criminal investigation in motion. Under the BNSS, information can also be given electronically (e-FIR).

An FIR registered at any police station regardless of where the offence took place, later transferred to the station with jurisdiction. The BNSS recognises this so that no complaint is turned away for territorial reasons.
An offence in which the police may register an FIR, investigate and arrest without prior permission of a court — generally the more serious offences, such as theft, robbery or murder.
An offence in which the police cannot investigate or arrest without the order of a Magistrate — generally less serious offences, such as simple defamation.
In a bailable offence, release on bail is a right. In a non-bailable offence, bail is at the discretion of the court — not automatic, and not impossible.
A direction that a person who fears arrest be released on bail if arrested, sought in advance under Section 482 of the BNSS.
The guilty mind: the intention or knowledge behind an act. Most serious offences require both a wrongful act and a culpable state of mind.
The guilty act: the physical act (or unlawful omission) that a criminal offence requires, as distinct from the mental element.
Doing anything with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another.
Doing a thing with intent to defraud — to deceive, and by deception induce another to act to their loss or injury.
Property of every description except land and things attached to the earth, or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth.
Wrongful gain is gain, by unlawful means, of property to which the gainer is not legally entitled. Wrongful loss is loss, by unlawful means, of property to which the loser is legally entitled.
The police report filed in court after investigation, setting out the evidence and the offences alleged. Filing timelines are tied to the accused's right to default bail.
A summons is a court order to appear. A warrant is a court order authorising the police to arrest and produce a person. Which issues first depends on the seriousness of the case.
Property gifted to a woman before, at, or after marriage that remains her exclusive property. Dishonestly withholding it can amount to criminal breach of trust.
Unpaid public work ordered as punishment. Introduced as a formal punishment by the BNS for offences such as first-time petty theft (on return of the property) and defamation.

Wilful conduct likely to drive a woman to suicide or cause grave injury to her life or health (mental or physical), or harassment tied to unlawful demands for property. Defined for the offence of cruelty by a husband or his relatives.

caseLaws.title: Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar
caseLaws.principle: Cheating requires dishonest intention at the very start of the transaction — a promise that fails later is breach of contract, not cheating.
caseLaws.summary: The Court distinguished mere breach of contract from the offence of cheating. What matters is the accused's intention at the time the promise was made: if the intention to deceive existed from the beginning, cheating is made out; if the deal simply went bad later, the remedy is civil, not criminal.

caseLaws.title: Pyare Lal Bhargava v. State of Rajasthan
caseLaws.principle: Even a temporary taking without consent can be theft — permanent deprivation is not required.
caseLaws.summary: A government clerk removed an official file from his office for a day and returned it. The Court held that dishonestly moving property out of another's possession even temporarily satisfies the definition of theft.

caseLaws.title: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra
caseLaws.principle: Grave and sudden provocation is judged by the standard of a reasonable person, and the fatal act must follow before passion has time to cool.
caseLaws.summary: The celebrated naval-officer case examined when culpable homicide is not murder because of provocation. The Court held the exception is unavailable where there is time to cool off and the act is deliberate and planned.

caseLaws.title: Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab
caseLaws.principle: For murder it is enough that the injury intentionally inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
caseLaws.summary: The Court laid down the classic four-step test for the third clause of the murder definition: prove the injury, prove it was intended, and if that injury is objectively sufficient to cause death, the offence is murder — whether or not the accused knew how deadly it was.

caseLaws.title: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
caseLaws.principle: The death penalty is constitutional but reserved for the rarest of rare cases, where the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.
caseLaws.summary: A Constitution Bench upheld capital punishment for murder while confining it to the rarest of rare cases. Courts must weigh aggravating and mitigating circumstances relating both to the crime and to the criminal before choosing the death sentence.

caseLaws.title: Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab
caseLaws.principle: Set out the categories — manner, motive, magnitude and victim — for judging when a murder is rarest of rare.
caseLaws.summary: Building on Bachan Singh, the Court listed practical categories for the rarest-of-rare test: exceptionally brutal manner, depraved motive, anti-social magnitude, and vulnerable victims. It remains the working framework for death-sentence hearings.

caseLaws.title: State of A.P. v. R. Punnayya
caseLaws.principle: Culpable homicide is the genus and murder the species — all murder is culpable homicide, but not the reverse.
caseLaws.summary: The Court explained the three degrees of culpable homicide and gave a practical approach: first ask whether the act is culpable homicide at all, then whether it rises to murder, and only then which punishment tier applies.

caseLaws.title: Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab
caseLaws.principle: The right to life does not include a right to die; penalising abetment of suicide is constitutional.
caseLaws.summary: A Constitution Bench overruled the view that attempting suicide was protected by Article 21, and upheld the offences around suicide. The BNS later dropped the general offence of attempting suicide, keeping only the narrow case aimed at coercing public servants.

caseLaws.title: Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar
caseLaws.principle: Sedition provisions survive only if read narrowly: mere criticism of government is protected unless it incites violence or public disorder.
caseLaws.summary: The Court upheld the old sedition offence by confining it to acts with a tendency to incite violence or disorder. The BNS replaces sedition with a differently framed offence about endangering India's sovereignty, unity and integrity — the narrow-reading principle remains the key safeguard.

caseLaws.title: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab
caseLaws.principle: Doctors are criminally liable for negligence only where the negligence is gross — a mere error of judgment is not a crime.
caseLaws.summary: In a case about a patient's death in hospital, the Court adopted the Bolam standard: a medical professional acting in accordance with a practice accepted by a responsible body of the profession is not criminally negligent.

caseLaws.title: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
caseLaws.principle: Criminal defamation is constitutional: the right to reputation is part of the right to life.
caseLaws.summary: The Court upheld the offence of criminal defamation, holding that free speech under Article 19(1)(a) is not absolute and that reputation is protected as part of the right to life under Article 21.

caseLaws.title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
caseLaws.principle: No automatic arrests in cruelty cases: police must record reasons and follow a checklist before arresting for offences punishable up to seven years.
caseLaws.summary: Concerned by mechanical arrests in matrimonial-cruelty complaints, the Court directed police to apply an arrest checklist and magistrates to scrutinise detention, reinforcing that arrest is the exception, not the rule.

caseLaws.title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
caseLaws.principle: Section 66A of the IT Act struck down: vague restrictions on online speech are unconstitutional.
caseLaws.summary: The Court invalidated the offence of sending 'offensive' messages online for vagueness and overbreadth, while upholding narrowly framed cyber offences. A foundational judgment for online speech in India.

caseLaws.title: Rashmi Kumar v. Mahesh Kumar Bhada
caseLaws.principle: A wife's stridhan remains her exclusive property; a husband who dishonestly withholds it commits criminal breach of trust.
caseLaws.summary: The Court held that gifts given to a woman at marriage are her separate property. The husband holds them, if at all, as a trustee — dishonestly refusing to return them on demand can be criminal breach of trust.

caseLaws.title: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
caseLaws.principle: If information discloses a cognizable offence, the police must register an FIR — a preliminary inquiry is the exception.
caseLaws.summary: A Constitution Bench held FIR registration mandatory where a cognizable offence is disclosed, with limited categories — such as matrimonial or commercial disputes — where a short preliminary inquiry is permissible.

ipcMappings.note: Sedition as such is repealed. Section 152 creates a differently worded offence about acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India — the two are not identical.

situations.title: Road accident
situations.blurb: Injury, negligent driving and the police process
situations.intro: After a road accident, the law looks at how the vehicle was driven, whether anyone was hurt, and whether the driver stopped and reported. These provisions and terms explain the criminal side of a road accident. Insurance claims are a separate civil process.

situations.title: Money dispute
situations.blurb: Unpaid loans, broken promises and outright fraud
situations.intro: Not every unpaid debt is a crime. The law separates a deal that failed from a deception that was planned. These provisions explain when a money matter becomes cheating or breach of trust — and when it stays a civil claim under contract law.

situations.title: Online & cyber issue
situations.blurb: UPI fraud, identity theft and online impersonation
situations.intro: Online frauds usually combine an IT Act offence with cheating under the BNS. These provisions cover identity theft, impersonation through a phone or computer, and hacking-related acts.

situations.title: Property problem
situations.intro: Disputes about property range from trespass and damage to forced dispossession. Criminal law deals with dishonest or forcible acts; questions of ownership and title are decided by civil courts.

situations.title: Family matter
situations.blurb: Cruelty, dowry and protection within marriage
situations.intro: The criminal law protects spouses from cruelty and dowry-related harm. Divorce, maintenance and custody are civil matters under family law — those guides are being prepared for LexIndia.

situations.title: Workplace issue
situations.blurb: Harassment, threats and unpaid dues at work
situations.intro: Workplace problems can have both civil and criminal sides. Harassment and intimidation are offences; unpaid salary is usually a contractual claim. Start with what matches your situation.
